blocks.1: This is not meant as a contribution to the debate about where the “right” old Gulating site was. I only want to present some of what I have read and heard about Eivindvik in that connection. A great deal has been written and said about this; I have probably found only a small part of it, and lack of space means I must leave out much of the material I do have.
blocks.2: In the article mentioned earlier, Holck believes that the assembly was moved from Osen in Gaular to Gulen. He believes that the case between Berg-Onund at Ask and Egil Skallagrimsson was heard in Gaular, and writes that it is likely that “under the name of the Sogn Sea was included the stretch of sea from the southern shores of the Sognefjord right up to Atløy; indeed it is likely that this belonged to Sygnafylke,” and so believes that Eirik Bloodaxe sailed north along the “Sogn Sea” when he went after Egil, even though the assembly stood in Gaular. Holck then believes that the assembly was later, under Håkon Håkonsson, moved to Gulen and that the name was changed from Gaularting to Gulating. He thinks it likely that the assembly here stood in Eivindvik, and writes a little about how much better suited the parsonage must have been as an assembly site than “Gaulom, lying far inland. This must surely also have occasioned its move to Gulen.”
blocks.4: Dahl refutes the idea that the assembly stood north of the Sognefjord. He goes thoroughly into both what we find in the saga and in the Gulating law and compares it with everything we see in the landscape. In the article in “Det kgl. norske videnskabers selskabs skrifter”, p. 88, he writes, after quoting from Egil's saga: “Here it is said that the king had his men row north through the sound; that is still what the approach to Evenvik parsonage from the north is called, namely the parsonage or Evenvig sounds, and when it further says ‘and when he came to the Sogn Sea, Arinbjørn's men rowed in to Saudungssund’, hardly anyone who knows the area can be in any doubt about where both the king and Arinbjørn came from, nor about which way they went”. On page 90 he writes: “If it is denied that the Gulating was held south of the Sognefjord at this time, or the opposite is asserted, then all historical and geographical truth is denied as well, and with it all access to further inquiry.”
blocks.5: Dahl is, as mentioned, very thorough; his judgements are well founded and convincing. Gulen, or at any rate most of the area here, probably belonged to Nordhordland at that time, and all the others who have studied the site of the assembly on the basis of the text of the Gulating law also believe, as far as I have read, that the assembly must have stood in Nordhordland. (Brømel says on the border between Sogn and Hordaland.) One of the arguments in favour of this is that the “assembly travellers” from there received the least travel allowance, since they had such a short way to go. As far as I understand, there is now no disagreement either that the assembly stood in Gulen.
blocks.6: Dahl, as is well known, believed that the assembly site was in Eivindvik, on the parsonage land. He also believed, as mentioned, that old Gaulom, with the great heathen temple and well-known place of sacrifice, lay in the same place as the assembly. Brømel seems to agree with this in his article in Urda. On page 75 he writes that the place must have been well suited as an assembly site; he mentions the crosses, “which were presumably raised in place of the old idol temple when the White Christ had driven out Thor and the other idols”, he mentions “a holy spring” and the sacrificial grove, and writes: “so it is surely not without reason when one says: Dean Dahl is right in maintaining that the Gulating was held at and around Evindvig parsonage”. On p. 81 he writes about when Olav Tryggvason had the people baptised and Christianised at the Gulating in 997. “On this occasion, I presume, the old idol temple which stood at Gaulom was also torn down, the idols destroyed, the ancient venerable oak trunks of the sacred grove cut down, and first a stone cross raised, and later a Christian church built and consecrated where a heathen temple had stood before.”
blocks.7: Holm-Olsen says in an article in “Bergens Tidende” in July 1966: “If the assembly was in Eivindvik, we get the same link between assembly and church here as at the other regional assemblies. Personally I would rather believe that the assembly was first in Eivindvik, that this is the place the old Gulating law calls Guli, and that it was at this place until Håkon Håkonsson moved it to Guløy, that is, to a place near the church he built at Flolistrand”.
blocks.8: On p. 185 of his book Birkeli writes: “However, in going through the long debate about where the site of the Gulating was (see pp. 66–70), we have seen that it must be considered likely that Eivindvik in particular stands out as the place where the Gulating met, at least in the time when the kings Håkon Adalsteinsfostre, Olav Tryggvason, Olav Haraldsson and their missionaries worked to introduce Christianity into the country. This may throw light on the otherwise rather unmotivated placing of this cross. For if one looks at the terrain here in this hollow, one sees that the slope rises fairly steeply behind the cross. But just below it, and a little to the side of the spring, the ground forms a ‘platform’. Below this platform again there is plenty of room on a fairly level area without coming down to where the oak trunks were found. If one compares this situation with Thingvellir in Iceland, which is after all an offshoot of the Gulating, the parallel is striking. For the assembly did not gather on a large plain; it gathered on a plain facing a ‘platform’ and a slope, not least for the sake of the acoustics.” Further on the same page he writes: “If the assembly gathered as suggested here, the cross would in a way watch over the whole assembly. It is not strange that many, from Neumann and Dahl in the last century to Birknes in this one, believe that the assembly was held here and that the cross is connected with it. It is in connection with Dahl's assumption of the same that Neumann, when mentioning the cross, says that here ‘it is most likely that the assembly stood, as at the most solemn place’.”
blocks.9: He also quotes Karl Gåta like this: “The Gulating was presumably held by the northernmost cross up in the slope, where there is a large, even, gently sloping area on which several thousand people could easily find room.”
blocks.10: In an old newspaper cutting, for which I unfortunately have not found any date, an article about the “Raising of a memorial at the old Gulating site”, in which “the diocesan archivist Dr Just Bing and the bank secretary Skaasheim speak to ‘Dagen’”, says among other things:
blocks.11: “In August 1918 a committee consisting of Professor Magnus Olsen, the diocesan archivist Dr Just Bing, the landowner G.F. Heiberg and the bank secretary Anders Skaasheim inspected the various places in Gulen. After the inspection the committee unanimously concluded that Eivindvik must have been the old assembly site.”
blocks.12: By “the various places in Gulen” is meant the places here that the committee had learned might have been the old Gulating site. From information I have found elsewhere, it seems that the visit described here was made in connection with an inspection in Gulen by the working committee appointed to raise a Gulating memorial. Other people interested in history also took part, among them the newspaper editor Albert Joleik, who has written a good deal about the Gulating.
blocks.13: The article goes on to say that Dr Bing, who “at first held very firmly to Guløy”, now that he “came to the place and saw the conditions, found that Eivindvik was the only possible place”, and that “the committee unanimously holds to Eivindvik as the site of the Gulating”.
blocks.14: Knut Robberstad says in his paper on “Gulatinget”, p. 16, that the oldest assembly site may have been at Stemnebø or Kongshamn on Hisarøy. He also mentions that the assembly site may have been in Midtunvågen “on the western edge of the Midtun farm”, but believes that “by the time the country was Christianised, the assembly site must have been in Eivindvik”. He further believes that Håkon Håkonsson may, under pressure from the church, which by then had gained considerable influence, have moved the assembly to Byrknesøy or to Floli. Albert Joleik, who had family ties to Floli, believes that the assembly was first held at Midtun (in Midtunvågen) and then moved to the area by the church. Ivar Kleiva, who has studied and written a great deal about the Gulating, believes that the assembly was first held at Stemnebø, then moved to Eivindvik, where it stayed for the longest time, until Håkon Håkonsson moved it to Floli, and then after a short time it was moved again to Bergen.
blocks.15: THE RECORDS OF DAHL AND FURNÆS
blocks.16: In “Gula Tidend” for 26 and 29 April 1905 there is a record of statements from people in Gulen in answer to questions, among other things whether they had heard anything about a “regional assembly having been held anywhere in Gulen”. The questions were asked and the record made by Dean Dahl and the parish clerk Furnæs in March 1823. At Haveland they spoke with 6 men. Five of them said they had heard that there was supposed to have been an assembly at Stemnebø. One, Ole Thorsen, whose father came from Stemnebø (it says the father was born at Stemnebø), “assured them that the assembly did not stand at Stevnebø, but that those attending were summoned there, and at Segløen the judgements were to be sealed.” “About Guløe” they all testified that they had heard nothing about “this place” except that there was supposed to have been a battle between ancient warriors “who had fought there”, and one of those asked said he had heard that a king called “Gule” was supposed to have lived on “Guløen”.
blocks.17: All those asked at Haveland said that no church stood at Flolistranda. A church was to be built there, but at night the raft of timber was carried off to Eivindvik. On the other hand, they believed that a church had stood at “Næsstranden or Næsstølen? below the farm Næse. The churchyard still shows clearly”.
blocks.18: In the same section it says that one of those asked had heard that a church had stood at Hauge, “on the piece of land now called Instebøen”, and in the same line: “On closer inspection clear traces of a churchyard were also found both at Floliestranden and at Høye”. It almost looks as if Dahl must have meant Nesstranda/Nesstølen here, since it is these church sites (Nesstranda and Hauge) that those asked in this section testify to, and which were then presumably examined.
blocks.19: At Nedre Opdal they also spoke with a number of men (5 are named). One of them said he had heard from an old man at Kjelby that there had been a battle on “Guløen” “and an assembly as well”.
blocks.20: At Øvre Opdal a 68-year-old man said he had heard that the Gulating stood on “Guløe, and that a battle was fought there between ancient warriors.” At Hauge they met one man who said he had heard that the assembly was supposed to have stood at Haveland.
blocks.21: From what I have seen in the two issues of “Gula Tidend”, there was no one else who had anything to say about the Gulating. It appears that Dahl and Furnæs were both in Brandangersundet and on Byrknesøy. At Byrknes they spoke with an old pilot who was born on Lille Kvernøy. He too knew nothing about the assembly, but had heard “that a battle is supposed to have been fought on Guløen and that the stone crosses in Eivindvik were set up by Saint Olaf as targets”.
blocks.23: We do not know exactly when the assembly was moved from Gulen to Bergen; it may have happened before 1300. Given the meaning we see in the name Guløy, it need not mean that the church that Håkon Håkonsson may have built at Guløy was built at Flolid. According to Birkeli, the parish register for Gulen shows that L. Dietrichson believes it concerned a new church in Eivindvik. In the period before, and indeed after, Håkon was made king, there was much strife over the power to rule Norway. These were troubled times. From what I have read, I get the impression that there must have been very little activity at the Gulating site in this period. It seems as if the assembly had not gathered here for a long time. It was the king and the clergy who dominated the assembly then, and the kings surely had enough to deal with amid all the unrest. The constant struggles over who should hold power probably also meant there was little peace and opportunity for the king to gather people at the “proper” assembly sites, and so they tended to hold only the most necessary assemblies in more central and safe places such as Bjørgvin and Nidaros. On p. 94 of the article in the writings of “Det kgl. norske videnskabers selskab”, Dahl says that in “the saga of Magnus Barefoot's sons, in Hryggjarstykki chap. 116” “it can be seen that it was lawful for the Frostating to be held in the town of Nidaros instead of at the usual place at Frosta. In the same way the Gulating was no doubt held in Bergen.”
blocks.24: In Ole Andreas Øverland's great historical work “Illustreret Norges Historie”, published in 1895 in 12 large volumes, there is something in volume 3, p. 381, that I find interesting in this connection. It concerns the choice of Håkon Håkonsson as king. At a “meeting of the king's men”, probably in Nidaros, Vegard Veradal said on behalf of the king's men that, until the Øreting could be convened, they wished Håkon to be called “king-elect”. “If you will not agree to this, then tomorrow we put our ships to sea and sail south to Bergen. There we summon the Gulating to take him as king, and so we place his cause and ours in the hands of God and the holy King Olaf”. This was in 1217.
blocks.25: At “a general assembly in Bergen” on “the Day of the Selje Martyrs (8 July)” they agreed that Håkon Håkonsson should be king. “Sigurd of Onarheim” spoke on behalf of “all the men of the Gulating”. Dagfinn Bonde also spoke for Håkon.
blocks.26: Filip, the Bagler king in “Viken”, wanted Norway to be divided between himself and Earl Skule. “A general meeting of the realm” was to be held the following summer, and the matter should be settled there. The bishops and all the leading men of the country were to be summoned to this meeting. The meeting was held in Bergen in 1218. There, as we remember from history, Inga, the king's mother, underwent the ordeal of carrying hot iron. For Håkon this turned out well: doubt that he was a king's son was cleared away, and a settlement was reached with Skule. At a new meeting of the realm in Bergen in 1223 Håkon was recognised as rightful heir to the throne and king, and yet another settlement was made with Skule.
blocks.27: Perhaps the assembly was not held in Gulen at all in these troubled and difficult years? Dahl and others have suggested this, and it seems quite likely when we consider how things were. If Nidaros was used as the assembly site for the Frostating, it was surely even more natural that the sessions of the Gulating in these difficult times were held in Bjørgvin, the largest and most important town. When the assemblies were not held here in Guli, perhaps the assembly church fell into disrepair. Håkon Håkonsson was probably informed where the proper assembly site was, and when he got a firm grip on the government of the country he moved the sessions back here and rebuilt the church. Perhaps he also placed the assembly closer to the church? Royal power and church power had become more of a state power. Håkon Håkonsson was concerned to improve relations with the church and tried to heal the conflict that had prevailed since the excommunication of King Sverre, among other things by protecting the church buildings. The legal system had probably also become more influenced by foreign culture and government. The church's officials gained more say, and the king probably also let his servants, for example the lawmen, take on more tasks. Many cases were decided elsewhere than at the assembly. By that time the assembly had probably become much smaller, both in the number of cases and in attendance; the clergy and the crown now decided many of the cases, so the space below the slope north of the church, next to the “Lovseieberget” (the law-speaking rock), was probably large enough to hold the much reduced sessions.
blocks.28: The son of one of those who helped dig out the foundations when a new barn was built at the parsonage (1895) told me that during the work they found a large wooden table. The table was so rotten that they simply broke it up. Bjordø also tells in his book that a table was found there. He also says that a number of logs were found that “could almost be counted as a kind of block chairs”. This agrees well with Westerlund's “visions”. I have also heard that remains of a ve-band (the cord marking off the sacred assembly area) are supposed to have been found. In the parish register for Gulen, the parish priest Hovden wrote that in connection with the search for the third cross in 1936 they also looked for the table mentioned, which may perhaps have been an assembly table, but without result. They found only some oak logs.
blocks.30: Stein Sandemose Bårdsen, who lives in Smådalen near Brosvik, says that around 1990 he had a visit from a man from Algeria. This man told him that at primary school in Algeria he learned that the Gulating was the oldest democratic court in the world.
blocks.31: The Gulating was probably the most important assembly in our country in the saga age. Brømel believes the assembly was founded by Harald Fairhair, whom he sees as “an excellent king who, through courage and wisdom and favoured by fortune, made Norway, until his time split into many small states, into a great and mighty kingdom.” Before his time the Gulating, “regarded as a general assembly, may not have existed; immediately after his time it is found mentioned”. Brømel further believes that when it says that Håkon Adalsteinsfostre gave the Gulating law, it probably means that with the help of Torleif the Wise's legal knowledge he gathered, and perhaps improved and changed, the laws previously used at the Gulating, and then laid the new collection of laws before the farmers and had it approved. The approval is said to have been unanimous, Brømel says. He believes that Håkon Adalsteinsfostre had men at his court who could write and had the law written down. In the article in “Urda” mentioned earlier, p. 80, he writes: “And now the chronicle says expressly of Olaf the Holy: the king summoned to him the wisest men in the land and had Håkon Adalsteinsfostre's law read out to them, and after taking away or adding what he saw fit, the farmers promised to abide by this law. He had it read out to them; it was therefore written.”
blocks.32: The character “þ” (or “thorn”, pronounced like the English “th”) is the first initial of the Gulating law. This beautiful initial can symbolise the Gulating – the Millennium Site of Sogn og Fjordane.
blocks.33: Brømel, then, believes that Harald Fairhair founded the Gulating and that Håkon Adalsteinsfostre had the Gulating law written down. After Harald Fairhair's unification, the western counties were presumably still the most important part of the country. He inherited Sygnafylke from his father, Halvdan the Black, who according to Brømel had worked on a law called the “Heidsivia law”. It may be that when Harald Fairhair came to rule the whole of Western Norway as well, the Gulating was used as the assembly, and Guli as the assembly site, for a much larger area than before, and that may be why it now became much better known throughout the country and is more often found “mentioned”, as Brømel says. But locally the Gulating and the Gulating law probably have roots reaching far back. The Althing in Iceland was founded around 930, Robberstad says. This assembly had the Gulating as its model, so by that time the assembly system and the law here must have been so well established that they could serve as a pattern the emigrants to Iceland took with them. The assembly and the law probably grew from a beginning in the time when people stopped being roaming hunters, settled in communities of farmers and needed laws and rules to regulate relations between them. The assembly held both legislative and judicial power: here the laws were adopted and here breaches of the law were judged.
blocks.34: There are various opinions on when the law was written down. Brømel believed, as mentioned, that it was already done under Håkon Adalsteinsfostre, while Professor Robberstad leans towards the view that it may have happened under St Olav, or that Olav had part of it written and the rest was written under Magnus the Good, or later in the 11th century. The oldest written legal text we know of is, according to Robberstad, the law of Olav, after St Olav.
blocks.35: The Gulating with its law gradually came to cover larger and larger areas. At its greatest the Gulating embraced the whole country from the Agder counties in the south to Sunnmøre in the north. Valdres, Hallingdal and Setesdal also belonged to it, as did the islands in the North Sea until they got their own law district. It might have been appropriate here to say something about the attendance the law required from the various counties, but I think that would take far too long. I will only mention that quite a lot of people could gather for a session; I have seen up to 1,000 people mentioned somewhere. It was not only those who attended because of the cases heard here who came to the assembly – in addition to the appointed members, the parties and the witnesses, many came to trade. They bartered for everyday goods, weapons, ornaments and much more. Many also came to make agreements, to meet kinsmen and friends, to hear the news, or simply to relax. Brømel also writes that the sessions were used for announcements of various kinds, and in time weights, measuring vessels and measures of length were also calibrated. When the district officials came home from the assembly, they were to summon an assembly in their own district to report on what had happened at the assembly and to calibrate measures and so on. Many of the great men came to the assembly with large retinues. They brought both servants and thralls, and much equipment, even animals, and of course plenty of food and drink.
blocks.36: Robberstad says that the Gulating met once a year. Under the law of Olav, the session began on the Thursday after Easter. Later the first day of the meeting became St Peter's Eve, 28 June, and then, under the law of 1274, 17 June, which was St Botolph's Day. (This day is said to have been a holy day in Setesdal right up to 1850.)
blocks.37: Brømel has written a good deal about how the assembly site was laid out and says that according to Egil's saga the assembly site lay on a wide field and a large idol temple stood nearby. (I have also read somewhere that there was a circle of large trees at the assembly site.) In this temple the judges, the parties and the witnesses swore the holy oath before going out onto the assembly field. On the altar of the temple lay a large ring. After the ring had been sprinkled with blood from the sacrificial animals, the one swearing the oath took the ring in his hand and spoke the following formula: “So help me Freyr and Njord and the almighty Ás (Odin), as I shall pursue this case, or defend myself in it, or bear witness, or pass judgement, as I know to be most right, most true and most according to the law.”
blocks.38: After Christian law had been introduced into the Gulating law, the oath was taken according to Christian ritual, with the hand laid on the Bible.
blocks.39: On the first Sunday of the session it was customary to free a thrall. A session could last for weeks, depending on how many cases there were to deal with. The lawman was a very important person at the Gulating: he recited the laws and presided over the assembly. Robberstad writes on p. 15 of the paper mentioned earlier that the assembly site had a law rock, “that is, a place where the lawman could stand and speak to the people. The people stood down the slope and on the assembly field below. The lawman was to face east, or in an easterly direction, when he spoke to the people.” As an example of what the lawman's opening speech might be like, I will quote from Professor Robberstad's article on the Gulating mentioned above: “In the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Here I today set a general law assembly with all the honour and dignity of an assembly that a fully empowered law assembly should have according to the law. Herewith I today set truce and full assembly peace among all men who have come here or may come while this law assembly lasts, and until each has come home again, forbidding each and every one to commit killing or harm or to injure anyone by word or deed. Whoever breaks this truce shall have forfeited property and peace, land and chattels, and never be able to atone for it. May this law assembly now sit like all others, with decency and good custom, so that it is pleasing to God and useful to us. Amen.”
blocks.40: The Gulating law is regarded as a very good and democratically constructed law. The law was revised several times, and the law book that Magnus the Lawmender had made, which was adopted at the Gulating in 1274, came to apply to the whole country and remained in force until Christian V issued his Norwegian Law in 1687. One may well say that the ideas of the Gulating law have been carried forward right up to our present Constitution. It has been said, as strongly as this, that the cradle of democracy in Norway stood in Gulen. The Gulating law has been translated into Danish, German and English.
blocks.41: There is a tradition that the decisions of the Gulating were sealed on Segløya. Holck says, in the article mentioned earlier, that people outside the district here called Segløya “Dragerøen”. He also says that there were houses on Segløya, which tradition confirms, and that the walls of these houses were taken to Vesetvik (what is now called Hausevik, after the first curate in Eivindvik parish, who was called Haugs and lived there) and used in a building. That is supposed to have happened about 60 years before the article was written, that is, around the 1760s.
blocks.42: Could the fact that the island was called “Dragerøen” have something to do with drawing in the sails? If so, I would like to mention what Anna Elisabeth Westerlund said about Stemnebø, namely that there had been a watch post in the area there. Perhaps Segløya was then part of this watch system, and people going to or coming from the assembly had to draw in their sail to be checked – lowering the sail for inspection on the way in, hoisting it after inspection on the way out.
blocks.43: I would also like to mention Stafsneset. Staff meant a marker. A marker must have stood on this headland, perhaps the one that marked the sailing approach to the Gulating site.
blocks.44: Before the assembly system in Iceland was established, around 930 AD, the Icelanders sent a man, Ulfljot, to Norway to study the conditions at and around the Gulating and the Gulating law. He was in Norway for 3 years, and when he came back the assembly site at Thingvellir was laid out on the pattern of the Gulating. As mentioned, Birkeli says in his book, p. 185, that the parallel between Thingvellir and the area at Krossteigen is “striking”. I believe all of us who have visited Thingvellir must agree. The likeness becomes even greater when we also compare the position of the church and the older parsonage buildings here with the conditions at Thingvellir. Another thing that also fits the area here well in comparison with the assembly in Iceland is what I quoted earlier from Knut Robberstad's paper on the Gulating, p. 15, that “the people stood down the slope and on the assembly field below”.
blocks.45: Per Linge (compare the sections on the name and on the stone crosses), who compares our history (including what we have from Snorri) with Turkic and Roman history, believes that it was in the heyday of the Turks/Huns that Eivindvik began and developed as a historic site, according to Turkic rules and guidelines. He calls the place a city under a Turkic system of government with legislative power, Scandinavia's oldest capital. At that time it was usual for such capitals to be enclosed, as here with the great stone wall that still stands. Eivindvik was very strategically and centrally placed when one thinks of the opportunity to exercise control along the traffic routes: the coast, the Sognefjord, on to the inner valleys, to Lake Mjøsa and to Sweden (Uppsala). He had a theory that the Gulating developed here, under Turkic influence, from long before the time of Harald Fairhair.
blocks.46: Many years ago I heard of “Stjornvelta north of Bjørgvin”. Stjorn means government, and having now heard Linge's ideas and theories, I think it natural to connect this with what he says about the Huns, who ruled over large parts of Europe, probably having an important hub here where the senators/priests were responsible for ceremonies and government.
blocks.47: From what we read and hear, it seems that Eivindvik was an ancient gathering place where people from a large area had their sanctuaries for a long, long time. To me it also seems that the Gulating must have stood here, at least for most of the time before the assembly was moved to Bergen for good.
